days.title: Incomplete Dominance & Codominance
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define incomplete dominance.
  • Define codominance.
  • Differentiate these from complete dominance.
  • Predict offspring ratios.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Incomplete dominance — heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype.
  • Codominance — both alleles expressed distinctly.
  • Complete dominance — one allele masks the other.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Incomplete Dominance

Red flower (RR) × White flower (WW) → All Pink (RW). The heterozygote shows a blend.

B. Codominance

Red flower (RR) × White flower (WW) → Red AND White patches (RW). Both alleles expressed.

C. Human Example

  • AB blood type — codominance (A and B both expressed)
  • Sickle-cell trait — codominance at the molecular level

D. Comparison

PatternHeterozygote Phenotype
Complete dominanceDominant trait only
Incomplete dominanceIntermediate (blended)
CodominanceBoth traits expressed

💬 Let's Discuss

Mendel's peas showed complete dominance: in a heterozygote, one allele completely masks the other (Tt looks exactly like TT). But many traits do not follow this rule. There are two important exceptions.

In incomplete dominance, neither allele fully masks the other, so the heterozygote shows an intermediate or blended phenotype. In four-o'clock plants and snapdragons, red (RR) × white (WW) gives all pink (RW) flowers. The single R allele makes only enough pigment for pink. Crossing two pinks (RW × RW) gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white — here the phenotypic ratio matches the genotypic ratio, because each genotype looks different. Notice the red and white reappear, which proves the alleles never actually "mixed"; they only shared expression.

In codominance, both alleles are fully and separately expressed. A red bull × white cow can produce a roan calf whose coat has both red hairs and white hairs side by side — not pink hairs. In humans, a person with genotype IᴬIᴮ has type AB blood: red blood cells carry both the A and the B markers. People with sickle-cell trait (one normal and one sickle allele) make both normal and sickle hemoglobin, an example of codominance at the molecular level.

A quick test: look at the heterozygote. If it is in between (pink, wavy hair between curly and straight), it is incomplete dominance. If it shows both parental traits at once (spots, patches, two markers), it is codominance.

Common mistake: calling a speckled or spotted flower "incomplete dominance." Patches of both colors mean codominance.

pairs.why: In complete dominance, the dominant allele hides the recessive one.
In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote is intermediate between the parents.
In codominance, both alleles show up fully in the heterozygote.
Red × white giving pink flowers is incomplete dominance.
Red × white giving red-and-white patches is codominance.
Type AB blood shows both A and B markers — codominance.

scenarios.explanation: All-pink offspring are intermediate — incomplete dominance.

scenarios.text: Red × White → Red AND White patches.
scenarios.explanation: Separate red and white patches mean both alleles show — codominance.

scenarios.text: AB blood type shows both A and B.
scenarios.explanation: Both A and B markers appear in type AB — codominance.

scenarios.text: Heterozygote shows a blend of parental traits.
scenarios.explanation: A blend of the parental traits is incomplete dominance.

scenarios.text: Sickle-cell trait shows both normal and sickled cells.
scenarios.explanation: Both normal and sickle hemoglobin are made — codominance.
Pink × pink gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

questions.text: In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote shows:
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype.

questions.text: AB blood type is an example of:
questions.explanation: AB blood shows both A and B antigens — codominance.

questions.text: Which pattern shows BOTH alleles expressed distinctly?
questions.explanation: Codominance shows both alleles distinctly at the same time.

takeaways: Complete dominance = one allele masks the other.
AB blood type is an example of codominance.

days.title: Multiple Alleles & Polygenic Traits
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define multiple alleles.
  • Describe the ABO blood group system.
  • Define polygenic inheritance.
  • Give examples of polygenic traits.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Multiple alleles — more than two alleles in a population.
  • ABO blood group — 3 alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i.
  • Polygenic trait — controlled by multiple genes.
  • Continuous variation — a range of phenotypes.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Multiple Alleles — ABO Blood Type

GenotypeBlood Type
IᴬIᴬ or IᴬiA
IᴮIᴮ or IᴮiB
IᴬIᴮAB
iiO

B. Polygenic Traits

  • Height, skin color, eye color
  • Show continuous variation
  • Each gene adds a small effect

C. Other Modifications

  • Epistasis — one gene masks another
  • Pleiotropy — one gene affects multiple traits

💬 Let's Discuss

So far each gene had only two alleles. In a population, though, a gene can have multiple alleles — more than two versions — even though each person still carries only two of them.

The best-known example is the ABO blood group, controlled by one gene with three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ, which are codominant to each other, and i, which is recessive to both. This gives six genotypes and four blood types: Type A = IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi; Type B = IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi; Type AB = IᴬIᴮ; Type O = ii. Blood type matters in transfusions: type O can donate red cells to all types; type AB can receive from all. Blood typing was once used in paternity cases: for example, a type AB parent cannot have a type O child, because the child would need an i allele from each parent.

Polygenic traits are controlled by many genes, each adding a small effect. Human height, skin color, eye color and intelligence are polygenic. Instead of a few clear categories, they show continuous variation that forms a bell-shaped curve in a population: most people are medium height, few are very tall or very short. The environment also matters — nutrition affects height, and sun exposure affects skin tone.

Two related terms: pleiotropy is when one gene affects many traits (the sickle-cell allele affects blood cells, organs and resistance to malaria), and epistasis is when one gene affects the expression of another.

Common mistake: confusing "multiple alleles" (one gene, many versions) with "polygenic" (many genes, one trait).

pairs.why: Multiple alleles means a gene has more than two alleles in a population.
The ABO gene has three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i.
Type A can be IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi.
Type B can be IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi.
Type AB is IᴬIᴮ because Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant.
Type O requires two recessive i alleles.
A polygenic trait is controlled by many genes.

scenarios.explanation: Type AB is IᴬIᴮ.
Type O must be ii.
Heterozygous type A is Iᴬi.

scenarios.text: Skin color shows a range of tones.
scenarios.explanation: A range of skin tones comes from several genes — polygenic.

scenarios.text: Height varies continuously in a population.
scenarios.explanation: Continuous variation in height is polygenic.
One gene affecting many traits is pleiotropy.

questions.text: How many alleles control the ABO blood group?
questions.explanation: The ABO group has three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i.

questions.text: What is the genotype for blood type O?

questions.explanation: Height is controlled by many genes — polygenic.

takeaways: Epistasis = one gene masks another; Pleiotropy = one gene, many effects.

days.title: DNA & RNA Structure
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the molecular structure of DNA.
  • Describe the structure of RNA.
  • Compare DNA and RNA.
  • Explain base pairing.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Nucleotide — sugar + phosphate + base.
  • Double helix — DNA's twisted ladder structure.
  • Base pairing — A–T, G–C (DNA); A–U, G–C (RNA).
  • Antiparallel — strands run in opposite directions.

📚 Lesson Content

A. DNA Structure

  • Double-stranded helix
  • Sugar: deoxyribose
  • Bases: A, T, G, C
  • Base pairing: A–T, G–C
  • Antiparallel strands

B. RNA Structure

  • Single-stranded
  • Sugar: ribose
  • Bases: A, U, G, C
  • Base pairing: A–U, G–C
  • Three types: mRNA, tRNA, rRNA

C. DNA vs RNA

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
StrandsDoubleSingle
BasesA, T, G, CA, U, G, C
FunctionGenetic storageProtein synthesis

💬 Let's Discuss

Genes are made of DNA, and to understand how genes work you need to know its structure. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick built the double-helix model, using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.

DNA is a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). Sugars and phosphates link to form the sides of a twisted ladder — the double helix. The rungs are base pairs held by hydrogen bonds, following strict complementary base pairing: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G–C (3 hydrogen bonds). So if one strand reads ATGC, the other must read TACG. This is why the amount of A always equals T, and G equals C (Chargaff's rule). The two strands run in opposite directions — they are antiparallel (one 5'→3', the other 3'→5').

RNA differs in three ways: its sugar is ribose, it uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (so A pairs with U), and it is usually single-stranded. There are three main types: mRNA carries the gene's message from the nucleus to the ribosome; tRNA carries amino acids; rRNA forms part of ribosomes.

Think of DNA as the master cookbook kept safely in the library (nucleus), and mRNA as a photocopy of one recipe taken to the kitchen (ribosome).

Common mistake: pairing A with U in DNA. In DNA, A pairs with T; A–U pairs occur only when RNA is involved.

pairs.why: A nucleotide is a sugar, a phosphate and a base.
DNA's two strands twist into a double helix.
In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine.
Guanine pairs with cytosine in both DNA and RNA.
In RNA, adenine pairs with uracil.
The two DNA strands run in opposite directions.
mRNA carries the gene's message to the ribosome.

scenarios.explanation: Double-stranded nucleic acid is DNA.
Uracil is found only in RNA.
Deoxyribose is DNA's sugar.
A–T pairing occurs in DNA.
A–U pairing involves RNA.

scenarios.text: Carries genetic info from DNA to ribosome.
scenarios.explanation: mRNA carries the message from DNA to the ribosome.

questions.text: Which sugar is found in DNA?
Which base pairs with adenine in RNA?
questions.explanation: In RNA, adenine pairs with uracil.

questions.text: Which of the following describes DNA?
questions.explanation: DNA is double-stranded and contains deoxyribose.

takeaways: A–T and G–C in DNA; A–U and G–C in RNA.

days.title: Protein Structure & the Central Dogma
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe protein structure.
  • Explain the central dogma of molecular biology.
  • Define transcription and translation.
  • Relate DNA to protein function.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Central dogma — DNA → RNA → Protein.
  • Transcription — DNA → mRNA.
  • Translation — mRNA → protein.
  • Codon — 3 nucleotides that code for an amino acid.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Central Dogma

DNA → RNA → Protein. Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein.

B. Transcription

Occurs in the nucleus. RNA polymerase makes mRNA from a DNA template.

C. Translation

Occurs at the ribosome. mRNA codons are matched to tRNA anticodons, adding amino acids to a growing polypeptide.

D. Protein Structure

  • Primary — amino acid sequence
  • Secondary — alpha helices, beta sheets
  • Tertiary — 3D folding
  • Quaternary — multiple chains

💬 Let's Discuss

How does a sequence of DNA bases become a trait like eye color or a working enzyme? The answer is the central dogma of molecular biology: DNA → RNA → Protein. Information flows from genes to proteins, and proteins do the work that creates traits.

Transcription (DNA → mRNA) happens in the nucleus in eukaryotes. A gene's DNA is copied into a matching mRNA strand. "Transcribe" means to copy in the same language — both are nucleic acids.

Translation (mRNA → protein) happens at the ribosome in the cytoplasm. The mRNA is read in groups of three bases called codons; each codon specifies one amino acid. "Translate" means to change languages — from nucleotides to amino acids. With 4 bases taken 3 at a time there are 64 codons, more than enough for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons. The genetic code is nearly universal: the same codons mean the same amino acids in bacteria, plants and humans — which is why bacteria can be engineered to make human insulin.

The amino acid chain then folds into a protein with four levels of structure: primary (sequence), secondary (helices and sheets), tertiary (3D shape) and quaternary (several chains, like hemoglobin's four). The DNA sequence determines the amino acid sequence, which determines the shape, which determines the function — and ultimately the phenotype.

Common mistake: thinking DNA leaves the nucleus to make proteins. DNA stays inside; the mRNA copy travels to the ribosome.

pairs.why: The central dogma: information flows DNA → RNA → protein.
Transcription copies DNA into mRNA.
Translation uses mRNA to build a protein.
A codon is three bases that code for one amino acid.
Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids.
Quaternary structure is several polypeptide chains together.

scenarios.text: DNA is used to make mRNA.
scenarios.explanation: Making mRNA from DNA is transcription.

scenarios.text: mRNA is used to make protein.
scenarios.explanation: Making protein from mRNA is translation.
Translation takes place at the ribosome.
In eukaryotes, transcription happens in the nucleus.
Each codon specifies one amino acid.
Four subunits joined together is quaternary structure.

questions.explanation: The central dogma is DNA → RNA → protein.
